chapter: Retirement and the future of big bands
title: Why big bands will not come back: no new bands and arranging costs
summary: Arguing with Willard Alexander's optimism, Barnet says there are only ghost bands and old names, and copying and arranging costs make new bands impossible.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Willard says it is. Of course that's his business. Willard Alexander.
All right, where's his new bands?
Maynard Ferguson and his 13 angry men?
He said every band that he's handling has got a full itinerary, months ahead, and there's lots and lots of work.

Well, true, but who is he handling? He's handling ghost bands, the Glenn Miller Band, the Jimmy Dorsey Band, the Tommy Dorsey Band. Well, he's got Kenton and he's got Maynard Ferguson and Woody Herman. But where are the new bands, Pat? Where are they? There aren't any new bands. And this is the whole thing. I mean it's almost impossible today for a new band to get started. You could say Buddy Rich is a new band if you want to. But Buddy Rich is not a new band. Buddy Rich is an old name which a band was built around. But there are no youth people. Maynard Ferguson's an old name. He played with me, he played with Kenton. This is not new. And when you show me where there's a new band that's really

making it, or bands, let's put it that way, then you might say there might be a resurgence in the band business. Although I can't see economically where they could possibly make it. Even in our time there were angels. Maria Kramer at the Lincoln-Edison Hotel. She -- well, we were involved in a deal. She was involved with Jan Savitt. She was involved with Gray Gordon, with Blue Baron, owned a piece of the band in return for putting them in there and putting us in there, you know, for the air time, and she got a cut off the top until the union stopped it. You had A. Edward Masters, the attorney. He had two bands that he had financial investments in. Johnny Long and Jerry Wald. And they had investments up to $50,000.00 at that time, and neither one of them really got off the ground. Do you imagine what it would cost today to get a band off the ground, with the way -- like when you used to have an arranger on salary, you know, like $75.00 a week or something, or a hundred and a half if he was a real good arranger, for all he could turn out in that time. Today it'd cost you three or four times that just to get the arrangement copied, not to mention the guy that makes the arrangement. And then if you want to use it in a night club, that's fine, but if you want to record it you've got to pay them and the copyist all over again. If you want to make it in a movie you've got to pay the copyist and the arranger all over again. If you're going to play it on television you've got to pay the arranger and the copyist all over again. You wind up with over $2,000.00 an

arrangement. There's no way in the world that a new band can overcome those costs. That's why I say there will never be the big band business. Now when we -- God forbid -- when we lose the guys that are still out on the road, the names of anybody that is left there, there won't be any names left, and then where is your big band business? Willard is trading on what happened before. He's not trading on anything new. Period. I rest my case.
